title: Never Mistake a Correlation for a Cause
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article urges leaders to resist the mental shortcut of treating correlated variables as causal, especially when explaining human behavior and performance. Using the example of compensation and talent retention, it shows how a strong, well-known correlation gets treated as cause-and-effect for the sake of decision-making ease, even though multiple moderating factors, market conditions, manager relationships, promotion pathways, actually shape the outcome. The piece argues leaders default to false causal thinking not out of laziness but efficiency, since a causal story makes fixing a problem feel simpler than it is. It recommends starting the decision process by assuming any presented cause-and-effect claim is likely wrong, then actively hunting for the moderating variables underneath it.
points: Leaders default to treating correlations as causation because causal explanations make problems feel easier to fix, not because they're lazy.
The strong correlation between compensation and retention is moderated by multiple other factors, yet is routinely treated as simple cause-and-effect.
Good decision-makers start by assuming any presented "cause" is probably not the real driver, then search for what's actually moderating the relationship.
In the social world, effects nearly always have multiple causes, so leaders should keep looking for correlates even after finding a plausible list.
quotes: Good leaders and decision-makers maintain a healthy skepticism of cause-and-effect relationships.
For example, the correlation between talent retention and compensation is known to be strong. The more a team member is compensated, the more likely they are to stay in their seat.
Yet, leaders are highly tempted to view that relationship as causal. Not because they are lazy, but because they are efficient thinkers.
They begin the decision-making process with the assumption that whatever is presented as causal is likely not true.
In the social world, there are nearly always multiple causes to any effect.
